title: Scattered, and Still Chosen
sum: Psalm 9 is a confession. Israel was taken captive and scattered among the nations "just as God had said" (9:1-2), and the poet says this proves God right, for he is the righteous judge who sees every deed (9:3-6). Then comes the book's clearest word on human choice: what we do lies "in the choice and power of our own souls", and whoever does right stores up life with the Lord, while whoever does wrong brings on his own ruin (9:7-10).

The second half turns to mercy. God is kind to those who call on him; he washes clean the soul that confesses, and forgiveness is for sinners who are sorry (9:11-15). The psalm ends by holding God to his choice of Abraham's offspring and his covenant with the fathers (9:16-20). Choice and covenant stand side by side: people answer for their deeds, and God's mercy rests on his chosen people.
readings: Like Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9 and Baruch 1-2, the psalm answers disaster by confessing sin and declaring God just. The shame belongs to the people; the righteousness belongs to God (9:3, 9:13).
Read in the debate on grace and works

Readers of Paul have used this psalm as a window on Jewish thought in his day. It joins judgment by deeds (9:9) with God's choice of Israel and forgiveness for the repentant (9:14-19): the pattern E. P. Sanders called "covenantal nomism" (see the New Perspective topic). Others stress 9:7 and 9:9 as evidence that some Jews thought life was earned. The psalm itself holds both.

views.H: Gray reads the captivity of 9:1 alongside 2:3-15 and 8:24 as the exile of the Jews Pompey took west, so the psalm reworks the old language of the Babylonian exile for a new disaster. He saw in 9:7 one of the marks of Pharisee teaching.
views.J: Josephus says the Pharisees held that doing right or wrong lies mostly with people, though fate also acts (Jewish War 2.8.14), and Ryle and James set beside 9:7 the saying of Mishnah Avot, "Everything is foreseen; and freewill is given." The psalm's mix of choice, repentance and covenant is close to later rabbinic teaching.
views.N: Paul says God "will pay back each person according to his works" (Romans 2:6) and also that salvation "does not come from works" (Ephesians 2:9). Jesus came "to call sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32), the point of 9:14. The psalm gives the Jewish setting in which those sayings were heard.
views.P: The heading "for correction" and the confession of 9:3 echo Psalm 51:4. The close (9:16-20) is a lament-psalm appeal: we are your people; do not take your mercy away.
views.C: No church reads this psalm in worship as Scripture. For Christian debates on free will and grace, which this psalm does not settle, see the topic pages (free-will; justification); the site does not add a "Where Christians differ" card here, because no church's teaching addresses this psalm itself.

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:27; Deuteronomy 30:19; Psalm 51:4; Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:7; Sirach 15:14-17; Romans 2:6-7; Romans 3:4; Ephesians 2:8-10; Luke 5:32; Luke 15:7; Matthew 6:20

settings.what: A confession and an appeal for mercy
settings.by: A devout poet, speaking for Israel as "we"
settings.to: God, in the hearing of the devout gathered in Jerusalem
settings.when: After a scattering of the people into foreign lands; most likely the captivity that followed Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC (Gray)
settings.why: To accept the disaster as God's just judgment, to call each person to answer for his own choices, and to lean on the covenant with Abraham's offspring for mercy. Knowing that the speakers are survivors of a conquest makes the confession an act of faith, not a theory of free will.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: Happy Is the Man God Corrects
sum: Psalm 10 is a short hymn on discipline. Happy is the man the Lord rebukes and turns from the evil road with the whip, for the discipline cleans him of sin (10:1-2). The Lord makes straight the paths of the righteous and remembers his servants with mercy (10:3-4). The witness to this stands in the law and in God's visits to people (10:5).
The second half moves from the one to the many: Israel, the devout, the poor and the assemblies of Israel will praise the Lord, who is righteous, faithful, good and merciful forever (10:6-9).

views.H: Gray saw in the book's praise of discipline the outlook of "political quietists" who took the present distress as God's training. Ryle and James contrasted such patience with the Zealots' readiness to fight Rome.
views.J: Discipline as a father's love runs from Deuteronomy 8:5 and Proverbs 3:11-12 into later Jewish teaching on suffering as purifying. The "assemblies of Israel" (10:8) are gatherings for prayer, not yet synagogue buildings.
views.N: Hebrews 12:5-11 quotes the Greek of Proverbs 3:11-12 and makes the same argument for Christians: "God is dealing with you as his sons."
views.P: The psalm opens with the Psalter's "Happy is" (Psalm 1:1; 94:12) and closes with the doxology formula of the book (9:20; 11:9).

echoes: Job 5:17; Psalm 94:12; Proverbs 3:11-12; Deuteronomy 8:5; Hebrews 12:5-11; Psalm 145:17; Isaiah 35:10

settings.to: The devout and the poor of Israel, gathered in assembly
settings.when: In a time of hardship that the poet reads as God's correction
settings.why: To teach the hearers to welcome correction as a mark of God's love, and to keep them praising together while they wait for mercy.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: Jerusalem, Look East and West
sum: Psalm 11 is the book's song of homecoming. A trumpet sounds in Zion; a herald brings good news: God has had mercy on Israel (11:1-2). Jerusalem stands on a height and sees her children gathered from east and west, north and the far islands (11:3-4). Mountains sink to flat ground, hills run away, the woods give shade and God makes fragrant trees spring up along the road (11:5-7).

Jerusalem is told to put on her glorious clothes, for God has promised good things to Israel forever, and the psalm ends with a prayer that the Lord will do what he promised (11:8-9). Its heading calls it a psalm "for waiting in hope": the return is seen as if done, and prayed for as still to come.
readings: Baruch 4:36-5:9 says nearly the same things in the same order, often in the same Greek words (see the note at 11:3). Gray reports that Ryle and James accept that Baruch borrowed from this psalm and that Viteau rejects it, and he points to Ryle and James for how both passages relate to Isaiah 40-66. The site's Baruch notes give the views from Baruch's side.

Isaiah's road through the desert (Isaiah 40:3-5) and his trees in the wilderness (Isaiah 41:19) turn the return into a second Exodus. Luke uses the same Isaiah lines for John the Baptist (Luke 3:4-6).

views.H: Ryle and James used the relation of this psalm to Baruch to argue that the Greek translation was made before AD 70; Gray agreed on the date but doubted part of their argument, since Baruch 5:6 may itself be a translation from Hebrew.
views.J: Ryle and James place the psalm among Jewish texts that copy the prophets' picture of the return and add marvelous details. The hope of all the tribes gathered home is also in Psalm 17 (17:28-31, 17:50).
views.N: The herald "who brings good news" (11:2) is Isaiah's euangelizomenos, the root of the word "gospel". Jesus speaks of a great trumpet gathering his chosen (Matthew 24:31) and of many coming from east and west (Matthew 8:11).
views.P: The trumpet in Zion is Joel 2:1 turned to joy; the poem is built from Isaiah 40, 49, 52 and 60.

deep.h: Psalm 11 and Baruch 4:36-5:9 side by side
deep.b:
Both poems tell Jerusalem to stand on a height and see her children gathered from east and west (11:3; Baruch 5:5). Both have mountains brought low to level ground, the Greek homalismos (11:5; Baruch 5:7). Both have the woods giving shade and every fragrant tree (11:6-7; Baruch 5:8); Ryle and James note that "tree of sweet savor" occurs only in these two. Both dress Jerusalem in glory (11:8; Baruch 5:1-2).

Three explanations are offered. Baruch borrowed from the psalm: Gray reports that Ryle and James accept this. Baruch did not borrow from it: Gray reports that Viteau rejects that dependence. Both draw on Isaiah 40-66: Gray points to Ryle and James for how both passages relate to those chapters, and the site's note on Baruch 5:5 leaves the direction open. The question matters for dating Baruch more than this psalm, which Gray dates to the middle of the first century BC.

echoes: Joel 2:1; Isaiah 27:13; Isaiah 40:3-9; Isaiah 43:5-6; Isaiah 49:12; Isaiah 52:1-7; Isaiah 60:4; Baruch 4:36-5:9; Luke 3:4-6; Matthew 8:11; Matthew 24:31

settings.by: A devout poet, speaking as a herald
settings.to: Jerusalem, pictured as a mother waiting for her children
settings.when: While Israel was still scattered; the heading says it is "for waiting in hope"
settings.why: To make the promised return so vivid that the hearers could live in hope of it, and to turn that hope into prayer (11:9).
settings.readers: Devout Jews after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, still waiting for the scattered tribes to come home (11:2-7). Gray dates the collection to the middle of the first century BC, after 63 BC. This psalm also bears on when the Greek was made: Ryle and James argued from its likeness to Baruch 4:36-5:9 that the Psalms of Solomon were in Greek before AD 70. Gray reports that Viteau, who denies that Baruch borrowed from the psalm, reached the same date from the Greek style, while Gray himself warned that the argument fails if Baruch 5 was itself translated from Hebrew.

title: Against the Slanderer
sum: Psalm 12 asks God to rescue the singer from a law-breaking man whose whispering tongue spreads lies. His twisted words burn like a fire among a people; he fills houses with lies, cuts down "trees of gladness" and sets households against each other (12:1-4). The text of 12:2-4 is damaged, but the picture is clear.

The poet prays that the slanderer's lips be kept far from the innocent and his tongue destroyed, and that the Lord guard the quiet soul and the man who makes peace at home (12:4-6). It ends with salvation for Israel and the promises for the devout (12:7-8).

views.H: Ryle and James suggest the slanderer may have been a Sadducee who informed against a leading Pharisee at court, but add, "Further than this we cannot undertake to go." Gray notes the view of Ryle and James that Psalms 4 and 12, where the sinners are not yet punished, may be the oldest in the book.
views.J: Jewish teaching made slander a grave sin (Leviticus 19:16; Sirach 28:13-26). The "quiet soul" (12:6) is the devout ideal of peaceable faith.
views.N: James calls the tongue "a fire" (James 3:6), and Paul lists whisperers among sinners (Romans 1:29).
views.P: The psalm takes the shape of Psalms 12 and 120 of the Psalter, prayers against lying lips.

echoes: Psalm 12:2-3; Psalm 52:2-4; Psalm 120:2-3; Proverbs 16:28; Proverbs 26:20-21; Sirach 28:13; James 3:5-6; Romans 1:29

settings.to: The Lord, in the hearing of the devout
settings.when: When a slanderer was ruining households in the singer's community; Ryle and James think before Pompey's coming
settings.why: To hand the slanderer over to God instead of answering in kind, and to commend the quiet, peaceable life.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: Discipline and Destruction
sum: Psalm 13 thanks the Lord whose right hand sheltered the devout from sword, famine, death and wild beasts (13:1-3). Then it explains the difference between two kinds of suffering. The sinner's downfall is terrible and final; the righteous are disciplined privately, as a father corrects a son he loves, and their offenses are wiped out (13:4-9).

So the life of the righteous lasts forever, while sinners are carried off to destruction and forgotten (13:9-11). The difficult 13:4 reads "the ungodly man was shaken" in every manuscript; many scholars think it once said "the righteous" (see the variant).

views.H: Gray links the four threats of 13:2-3 with the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21 and takes them as the hardships of the war years.
views.J: Gray counts "scrupulous anxiety about sins done in ignorance" among the marks of the devout, and points to 13:4-6. The law's offerings for such sins (Leviticus 4) stand behind the thought.
views.N: Hebrews 12:5-11 makes the same contrast between a father's discipline and rejection; the hope of life forever for the righteous is close to John 5:28-29.
views.P: The "right hand" and "arm" of the Lord (13:1-2) are the Exodus images of the Psalter (Psalm 98:1).

echoes: Ezekiel 14:21; Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:12; Exodus 4:22; Leviticus 4:2; Hebrews 12:5-11; Daniel 12:2

settings.what: A thanksgiving and a teaching on suffering
settings.to: The righteous; the heading calls it "comfort for the righteous"
settings.when: After the devout had survived a time of war, famine and death
settings.why: To comfort the righteous that their suffering is a father's discipline and not the sinner's end, so that they will not lose heart.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: The Trees of the Lord's Garden
sum: Psalm 14 praises the Lord, faithful to those who love him, bear his discipline and live by the law he gave "so that we would live" (14:1). The devout are the Lord's paradise, his trees of life, rooted forever, for Israel is God's share (14:2-3).

The sinners are not so: they loved a short day of sin and forgot God, though he knows every heart. Their inheritance is Hades, darkness and destruction; the devout will inherit life with gladness (14:4-6).

views.H: Gray reads the psalm as the clearest sign that the devout hoped for blessed life after death, while for the sinners "all that awaits them after death is destruction in Sheol".
views.J: The law as the source of life (Leviticus 18:5) and Israel as God's share (Deuteronomy 32:9) are the psalm's foundations. Paradise as a picture of the righteous grew in later Jewish writing.
views.N: Revelation promises "to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7), and Jesus' story of the rich man puts the wicked in Hades (Luke 16:23).
views.P: The planted, rooted righteous are the tree of Psalm 1:3; the two ways of Psalm 1 are the psalm's plan.

echoes: Leviticus 18:5; Deuteronomy 32:9; Psalm 1:3; Psalm 92:12-14; Isaiah 61:3; Genesis 2:9; Revelation 2:7; Luke 16:23

settings.what: A hymn on the two ways
settings.to: The devout, who love the Lord and keep the law
settings.when: Not stated; the contrast with "the sinners" fits the party strife of the time
settings.why: To assure the devout that keeping the law is the way of lasting life, and that the sinners' pleasures end in Hades.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: God's Sign on the Righteous
sum: Psalm 15 begins as a thanksgiving: the singer called on the Lord in trouble and was saved (15:1-4). His new psalm is the "fruit of the lips" from a righteous heart, and whoever offers such praise will never be shaken (15:5-6).

Then the judgment: when the fire of the Lord goes out against sinners, God's sign is on the righteous to save them. Famine, sword and death run from the devout like people chased in war, and hunt down the sinners, who bear the sign of destruction on their foreheads (15:7-10). The sinners' inheritance is destruction and Hades; those who fear the Lord will live by his mercy (15:11-15).
readings: Ezekiel's mark on the faithful (Ezekiel 9:4) protects them in Jerusalem's fall; Revelation's seal on God's servants (Revelation 7:3) protects them in the plagues. The psalm stands between the two, and adds a mark on the sinners too (15:10).
The thanksgiving and the judgment belong together: the one who offers praise from a righteous heart (15:5-6) is the one marked for rescue (15:8).

views.H: The text of 15:9 is damaged: the words "chased in war" are a scholar's conjecture printed by Swete (see the variant).
views.J: Sword, famine and pestilence are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Jeremiah; the psalm pictures them as hunters who spare the devout.
views.N: Revelation's seal on the forehead and the beast's mark (Revelation 7:3; 13:16; 14:9) give the same two-sided picture.
views.P: "A new psalm" (15:5) is the Psalter's "new song" (Psalm 96:1).

echoes: Ezekiel 9:4-6; Exodus 12:13; Psalm 91:3-7; Hosea 14:2; Hebrews 13:15; Revelation 7:3; Revelation 9:4; Revelation 14:9

settings.what: A thanksgiving and a vision of judgment
settings.to: God, and the devout who hear the psalm
settings.when: After a rescue from trouble; the judgment looks to "the day of the Lord's judgment" (15:13)
settings.why: To give thanks, and to assure the devout that in the coming judgment God will know and save his own.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: I Nearly Slipped
sum: Psalm 16 is a personal testimony. The singer's soul grew drowsy and drifted from God until he nearly slid into death and stood near the gates of Hades with the sinner; then the Lord took hold of him with his mercy and jabbed him awake like a horse with a goad (16:1-5).

The rest is a prayer to stay awake: keep your mercy and the memory of you in my heart; keep me from evil sin and from the seducing woman; guard my hands, steps, tongue and temper; give me patience under discipline and contentment in poverty (16:6-15).

views.H: Gray took 16:12-14 as a sign that many of the devout were poor, and 16:7-8 as their abstention from the sexual sins they blamed on their opponents.
views.J: The prayer echoes Proverbs' warnings about the strange woman (Proverbs 5; 7) and the Psalter's "my feet had almost turned aside" (Psalm 73:2).
views.N: Paul's "I have learned to be content" (Philippians 4:11) and Hebrews on discipline (Hebrews 12:11) share its spirit.
views.P: The psalm borrows the wording of the Greek Psalm 73:2 ("nearly ... almost poured out") and has the shape of a thanksgiving followed by petitions.

echoes: Psalm 73:2; Psalm 94:18; Proverbs 5:3-5; Proverbs 7:21-23; Proverbs 30:8-9; Acts 26:14; Philippians 4:11-13; Hebrews 12:11

settings.what: A testimony and a prayer for protection
settings.to: God; the heading offers it "for help for the devout"
settings.when: After the singer had drifted from God and been brought back
settings.why: To warn the devout how easily faith grows drowsy, and to give them words for asking God to keep them.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.

title: Raise Up the Son of David
sum: Psalm 17 is the heart of the book. It opens and closes on God as King (17:1, 17:51). Between, it tells a story of loss. God chose David and swore that his royal line would never end (17:5). But sinners seized the throne God had not promised them and set up their own royal house (17:6-8). God then raised up "a man foreign to our race", who emptied the land, sent its people as far as the west and treated Jerusalem as the nations treat their cities (17:9-16). The devout fled to the deserts, the rain stopped, and from king to people all were in sin (17:17-22).

Then the prayer: "Look, Lord, and raise up for them their king, the son of David" (17:23). He will cleanse Jerusalem of the nations, drive out the sinners, smash their arrogance with an iron rod and conquer by the word of his mouth (17:24-27). He will gather a holy people, divide the land among the tribes, judge the nations and bring them to Jerusalem to see God's glory (17:28-35). He will trust in God, not in horses or gold; he will be pure from sin, made strong by a holy spirit, a shepherd who leads all as equals; and "their king will be the Lord Messiah" (17:36-47). "Happy are those who live in those days" (17:50).
readings: Read in its own setting, the psalm hopes for a human king of David's line. He is "taught by God" (17:35), girded with strength by God (17:24) and made strong by God's spirit (17:42), and the Lord is his King (17:38). Ryle and James saw in this picture "the merely human nature of the Messiah". He will free Jerusalem from Rome and from the unlawful kings, gather the tribes and rule the nations from Zion.

Christians read the psalm as a witness to the hope that Jesus fulfilled and changed. The Gospels call Jesus "son of David" (Matthew 1:1; 9:27; 21:9), Luke's angel announces him with the same two words as 17:36 (Luke 2:11), and Revelation gives him the iron rod of Psalm 2:9 (Revelation 19:15). But Jesus did not drive out the Romans; he spoke of a kingdom "not from this world" (John 18:36) and was crowned through the cross. The New Testament never quotes this psalm. The links are a shared hope and shared phrases, most of them drawn from the Hebrew Bible itself.

views.H: Most scholars, with Gray, read 17:5-20 as history: the Hasmonean priest-kings who took David's throne (17:6-8), Pompey as the foreign man (17:9) and the lawless one (17:13), and the captives taken to Rome (17:14). Gray reports that Frankenberg read 17:6 of the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem and 17:16 of Antiochus IV rather than Pompey; Gray rejected this. The psalm is usually dated soon after 63 BC.
views.J: The psalm is one of the fullest pictures of the Messiah son of David in Jewish writing before Jesus. It joins the promise of 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 89 with the king of Isaiah 11 and the shepherd of Ezekiel 34, and it hopes for the gathered tribes and a Jerusalem free of foreigners (17:28-31).
views.N: The phrases "son of David" (17:23), "the Lord Messiah" (17:36), the iron rod (17:26), the word of his mouth (17:27, 17:39), the twelve tribes judged (17:28) and "Happy are those who live in those days" (17:50) all have New Testament counterparts (see the notes). The site's notes on Luke 1-2 and 18-24 already cite this psalm for the hope of Jesus' hearers.
views.P: The king's portrait is built from Psalm 2 (the iron rod, the potter's jars), Psalm 72 (the nations serving), Psalm 89 (the oath to David), Deuteronomy 17 (no trust in horses or gold) and Isaiah 11 (the spirit, the word of his mouth). The two Selahs of the book come here and in 18:10.
views.C: Christian writers have valued the psalm as evidence of Jewish messianic hope before Jesus. It was copied in Greek Bible manuscripts and named in Codex Alexandrinus's list (Gray), but no church reads it as Scripture.

deep.h: What the son of David does, and what he does not do
deep.b:
What he does. He shatters unjust rulers and cleanses Jerusalem of the nations (17:24-25); drives out the sinners and smashes their arrogance (17:26); conquers by the word of his mouth (17:27, 17:39); gathers a holy people and judges the tribes (17:28); divides the land by tribes and keeps foreigners out (17:30-31); rules the nations and brings them to see God's glory (17:32-35); shepherds the Lord's flock in faithfulness and equality (17:45-46).

What he does not do. He does not trust in horse, rider or bow, or pile up gold and silver for war (17:37), keeping the law of the king that Solomon broke (Deuteronomy 17:16-17). He does not rule in his own strength: "The Lord himself is his King" (17:38). He is not called God or said to come from heaven; he is "taught by God" (17:35).

deep.h: Is he a man or more?
deep.b: Three lines raise the question. He is "pure from sin" (17:41), made "powerful by a holy spirit" (17:42), and called christos kyrios, "the Lord Messiah" (17:36). Ryle and James held that nothing in Psalms 17-18 gives him "any superhuman origin", and that kyrios here may stand for the Hebrew adon, "lord", a title for a king (Psalm 110:1), or for a misread "the LORD's anointed" (Lamentations 4:20). Gray chose the second. On either view the psalm describes a man, though an ideal one. Christians see in its sinless, Spirit-filled king a hope that only Jesus met (Hebrews 4:15), and the site's Luke 2:11 notes that Luke uses the same two words of him.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Luke's angel answers this psalm
deep.b: Luke 2:11 is the only place in the New Testament where the bare pair christos kyrios stands, as in 17:36; Luke 2:26 then has ton christon kyriou, as in 18:8 and the heading of Psalm 18. Luke's birth stories also share this book's words: people who wait for Israel's comfort and redemption (Luke 2:25, 2:38), mercy to Israel (Luke 1:54, 1:72), the arrogant scattered and rulers pulled down (Luke 1:51-52), as in 17:24 and 17:26, the throne of David (Luke 1:32). My suggestion is that Luke's angel speaks to shepherds in the very terms such devout Jews used, and then redefines them: the Lord Messiah is a baby in a feeding trough in David's town, and the shepherd-king of 17:45 comes first to shepherds. This is a theory about Luke's design, not evidence that Luke read this book. Ryle and James already noted that the angel may speak "in terms corresponding to the expectation" of his hearers.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Psalm 2:2; Psalm 2:8-9; Psalm 72:8-11; Psalm 89:3-4; Isaiah 11:1-5; Ezekiel 34:23-24; Deuteronomy 17:16-17; Lamentations 4:20; Luke 1:32-33; Luke 2:11; Matthew 1:1; Matthew 21:9; Mark 12:35-37; Acts 1:6; 2 Thessalonians 2:8; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15

settings.what: A royal psalm: lament for David's throne and prayer for the son of David
settings.to: The Lord, "our King", in the hearing of the devout
settings.when: After the Hasmonean kings had been brought down and Jerusalem taken by a foreign conqueror, most likely Pompey in 63 BC (Gray)
settings.why: To explain the disaster as God's judgment on kings who took a throne he had not promised them, and to keep alive the hope that God would keep his oath to David. Knowing the hearers had just lost both their own kings and their freedom shows why the psalm asks for a king who will cleanse Jerusalem of the nations: it is a prayer for liberation as much as for holiness.
settings.readers: Devout Jews in or near Jerusalem in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC. Gray dates most of the psalms soon after 63 BC and Psalm 2 soon after Pompey's death in 48 BC; he judged them the work of one hand or one generation, written in Hebrew ("now generally admitted") and soon read in Greek, before AD 70 on the view of both Ryle and James and Viteau.
views: The classic view (Gray; most scholars): the sinners are the Hasmonean rulers and the foreigner is Pompey.
Gray reports that Frankenberg referred 17:16 to Antiochus IV rather than Pompey; Gray thought the text weighs against it.

title: The Day of His Messiah
sum: Psalm 18 begins with God's mercy on all his works and his kindness to Israel, whom he disciplines as a father disciplines a firstborn, only son (18:1-5). It prays that God will make Israel clean for "the day of mercy", the day he has chosen to bring forward his Messiah (18:6), and it blesses the generation that will live "under the rod of discipline of the Lord's Messiah", guided in righteousness and the fear of God (18:7-10).

After a Selah the psalm turns to the sky. God set the lights in their courses, and they have never left the path he commanded, except when God gave orders through his servants (18:11-14). The poem stops there, without a closing blessing; Gray thinks its end is lost, and Ryle and James printed 18:11-14 as a separate psalm.

views.H: The heading "Again, of the Lord's Messiah" ties this psalm to Psalm 17. Ryle and James thought whoever wrote the titles may also have added the two Selahs (17:31; 18:10), to make the book look more like David's psalms. Gray notes that the Syriac manuscript he used breaks off at 17:38, so Psalm 18 survives only in Greek.
views.J: The Messiah here disciplines and guides Israel; the hope is for a purified people "in the days of mercy". Ryle and James saw no sign of a pre-existing Messiah in the word anaxis (18:6).
views.N: Simeon waits to see "the Lord's Messiah" (Luke 2:26), the phrase of 18:8; Jesus tells his disciples that their eyes are blessed to see what prophets and kings longed to see (Luke 10:23-24), the longing of 18:7.
views.P: The obedient lights recall Psalm 19:1-6 and Psalm 148:6; their one exception recalls Joshua 10 and Isaiah 38.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the lights are the model for the good generation
deep.b: Many read 18:11-14 as a separate poem. I suggest it may be the psalm's own conclusion. The coming generation will live "in the fear of God" (18:7-10); the lights walk "in the fear of God every day" (18:13) and "have not left the path you commanded them" (18:12). The sky shows what Israel will be under the Messiah: creation that keeps God's order, broken only at God's word. This overlaps with Ryle and James's remark that Jewish writers liked the theme of the order of the heavens, though they treated the verses as a distinct psalm; it is my reading, not theirs.

echoes: Exodus 4:22; Proverbs 3:12; Luke 2:26; Luke 10:23-24; Isaiah 11:2; Genesis 1:14-18; Psalm 148:3-6; Jeremiah 31:35-36; Joshua 10:12-14; Isaiah 38:7-8

settings.what: A prayer for the day of the Messiah, with a hymn on the lights of heaven
settings.when: In the same setting as Psalm 17, after the loss of Jerusalem's freedom
settings.why: To prepare Israel for the Messiah's coming by asking God to make them clean, and to show in the obedient sky the order the coming generation will keep.
settings.readers: Devout Jews after 63 BC who shared the hope of Psalm 17: the heading's "Again" and the repeated words "the Lord's Messiah" (18:0, 18:8; compare 17:36) join the two psalms, and Ryle and James list the expressions they share (wisdom, righteousness, strength, the rod). The last verses on the lights of heaven (18:11-14) change subject; Ryle and James thought them perhaps once a separate psalm, and Gray adds that the end seems to have been lost.
